PBS kills jobs that exceed their requested walltime even when the queue's 48-hour maximum has not been reached.
docs.title: Choosing CPU Count and Walltime

docs.text: Run nci_account before large jobs to confirm that the project has sufficient allocation remaining. It prints KSU (kilo service unit) usage and availability for your projects: nci_account These helper scripts are available under /scratch/pt17/.bin . If the commands are not found, set up the DAVE shared environment .
docs.title: Check the Available Allocation

docs.text: The qcost helper estimates the SU cost of a PBS job: qcost -c <cpus> -m <memory_GiB> -w <walltime_hours> -q <queue> For example, for 48 CPUs, 192 GiB, two hours, and the normal queue: qcost -c 48 -m 192 -w 2 -q normal
docs.title: Estimate a Job Before Submission

docs.text: Gadi charges jobs according to the resources reserved and the walltime used . The general formula is: Job Cost (SU) = Queue Charge Rate × max(NCPUs, Memory Proportion) × Walltime Used (hours) Where: Queue Charge Rate depends on the selected queue; express queues cost more per SU but increase priority. NCPUs is the number of requested CPUs. Memory Proportion is the requested memory divided by the queue's memory-per-core allowance (memory per node divided by CPUs per node). Requesting an outsized amount of memory can therefore increase the cost even if the job does not use it. A job requesting enough memory to fill a node effectively reserves the whole node and is charged accordingly. See the PBS job-cost documentation in the Gadi User Guide for the current queue charge rates and limits.
docs.title: Job Charging

docs.text: LPJ-GUESS uses well under 1 GiB of memory per CPU. Its costs are therefore normally dominated by CPU count rather than memory. The normal queue nodes have 48 CPUs and 192 GiB RAM, giving a memory-per-core ratio of 4 GiB/CPU. Because LPJ-GUESS memory use is below this threshold, the billing formula simplifies to: Job Cost (SU) = Queue Charge Rate × NCPUs × Walltime Used Requesting less than 4 GiB per CPU on the normal queue costs the same as requesting 4 GiB per CPU. Request 4 GiB per CPU as a safe default ; it does not cost more and avoids unexpected out-of-memory failures.
docs.title: Practical Implications for LPJ-GUESS

docs.text: LPJ-GUESS cost on Gadi is approximately 0.005–0.01 SU per patch . For a run over G gridcells, each containing P patches: estimated SUs ≈ G × P × 0.005 (lower bound) estimated SUs ≈ G × P × 0.01 (upper bound) The cost per SU is approximately $0.04 AUD (indicative—verify against current NCI pricing). These are first-order estimates assuming uniform patch runtime. More productive gridcells (higher biomass turnover) take slightly longer, but the effect is small and choose_num_cpus.py can minimise imbalance across workers. After a job finishes, compare this estimate with the actual cost recorded in the top-level job log. See Checking and Troubleshooting Gadi Runs .
docs.title: Estimating LPJ-GUESS Run Cost

docs.text: Setting Up Gadi Gadi is the HPC system at the National Computational Infrastructure (NCI) in Canberra. This page covers the one-time setup and background needed to run LPJ-GUESS DAVE jobs on Gadi. Once your account and environment are ready, continue with Running on Gadi . This guide is not a substitute for the comprehensive Gadi User Guide . Reading at least its sections on PBS, storage, and job debiting before your first run is strongly recommended. Connecting to Gadi ssh <nci_username>@gadi.nci.org.au Password authentication is possible but requires typing a password on every login, which is inconvenient for repeated sessions or scripted transfers. Setting up an SSH key pair is recommended for day-to-day use. To do this: Generate an ed25519 key pair if you don't already have one (see SSH Key Management ). Register the public key ( id_ed25519.pub ). Log in to Gadi with your password, then append your public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server. The easiest way is ssh-copy-id (Linux/macOS): ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub <nci_username>@gadi.nci.org.au You will be prompted for your NCI password once. After that, SSH and SFTP connections will use the key instead. If ssh-copy-id is not available (e.g. on Windows), log in manually and run: mkdir -p ~/.ssh && chmod 700 ~/.ssh cat >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys << 'EOF' <paste the contents of id_ed25519.pub here> EOF chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys Once the key is registered, ssh <nci_username>@gadi.nci.org.au will connect without a password prompt. Background: PBS Gadi uses PBS Pro (Portable Batch System) as its job scheduler. Rather than running programs directly, you describe the resources your job needs and submit it to PBS, which queues and executes it when resources become available. Concept Description Job A self-contained unit of work submitted via qsub Queue A named pool of compute nodes (e.g. normal , hugemem , express ) Walltime The maximum real-world time a job may run before PBS kills it Service Unit (SU) The unit of compute cost; jobs are billed to a project Project A budget account (e.g. pt17 ) that SUs are charged to Useful PBS commands: Command Description qstat -u $USER List your running and queued jobs qstat -f <jobid> Show detailed status for a specific job qdel <jobid> Cancel a job No single PBS job on Gadi may run for longer than 48 hours. See Choosing Gadi Resources and Estimating Costs for guidance on selecting CPUs, memory, and walltime. Environment Modules Software on Gadi is managed via the environment modules system. Rather than having one global version of each tool, multiple versions coexist and users activate the ones they need: module load netcdf # load the default netcdf version module load gcc/12.1.0 # load a specific version module list # list currently loaded modules module avail netcdf # list available versions of netcdf module show netcdf # show what a module does (paths it sets, etc.) module purge # unload all modules Module consistency The exact module versions loaded when compiling must also be loaded when running . Mismatching MPI implementations between build and runtime is a particularly common and hard-to-diagnose error. The build_gadi and submit_to_gadi.sh scripts ensure consistency; use them rather than loading modules manually. DAVE Shared Environment DAVE helper scripts and custom module files are available to all members of the pt17 group on Gadi. To make them available automatically at login, add this line to your own ~/.bashrc file: source /scratch/pt17/.bin/.bashrc That shared file adds /scratch/pt17/.bin to PATH , making the DAVE helper scripts available as normal shell commands. It also adds the DAVE custom module directory to MODULEPATH , so module avail and module load can see the project-specific modules. One of these modules is lpj-guess-utils , which provides Gadi-compiled versions of standard LPJ-GUESS utilities such as aslice , tslice , and gmap . Many of the shared helper scripts are maintained in the hol430/gadi-scripts repository. After editing ~/.bashrc , either log out and back in, or source it in the current shell: source ~/.bashrc Storage Gadi provides three types of storage, with very different properties. Home Directory ( $HOME ) $HOME ( /home/xxx/<nci_username> ) is limited to 10 GiB . It is intended for configuration files, scripts, and source code— never for job outputs . A run writing even modest output to $HOME will quickly exhaust the quota and cause jobs to fail. Scratch ( /scratch/<project>/$USER ) /scratch is the primary working space for job input and output. It is fast and has a larger quota, but files that have not been accessed or modified for 100 days are automatically deleted without warning. Files are first moved to a quarantine area before permanent deletion. Consult the Gadi User Guide linked above for instructions on listing and recovering quarantined files. No permanent storage The DAVE project does not have permanent storage on Gadi (only scratch). Important results should be backed up to HIE-Storage as soon as possible after a run completes. Gdata ( /g/data/<project> ) /g/data is persistent project storage not subject to the 100-day deletion policy. The DAVE project does not currently have any gdata allocation. PBS Filesystem Access PBS jobs must explicitly declare which filesystems they use, for example: #PBS -l storage=scratch/pt17+gdata/pt17 Accessing an undeclared path fails at runtime even if you can reach it interactively. The submit_to_gadi.sh script handles this automatically for standard runs; only manually written PBS scripts need to consider it. Check Storage Quotas with lquota The shared DAVE environment provides lquota , which prints storage usage and limits for each project you are a member of: lquota

docs.text: Checking and Troubleshooting Gadi Runs This page explains how to check a completed LPJ-GUESS DAVE job on Gadi and diagnose common failures. For building and submitting a job, see Running on Gadi . Start with the Job and Worker Logs The main job writes <job name>.log in the run directory. The bottom of this file contains the PBS resource summary, including the resources requested and used and the total job cost in service units (SU). Check this summary after each run, especially if the job took substantially more or less time than expected. For a model error or an unexpected scientific result, open the affected worker's runs/runX/guess.log first. The top-level job log is especially useful for PBS startup, resource, and walltime problems. The instruction file's verbosity controls each worker's model log: use at least 3 for informational messages, or 4 / 5 for more detail, and rerun if needed. See Start with guess.log for a search strategy. As a rough guide, LPJ-GUESS jobs should cost approximately 0.005–0.01 SU per patch , where: total patches = npatch × number of gridcells lower cost estimate = total patches × 0.005 SU upper cost estimate = total patches × 0.01 SU A cost significantly outside this range should be investigated. An unusually high cost may mean that work was duplicated between workers; an unusually low cost may indicate that the run did not process everything expected. See Estimating LPJ-GUESS Run Cost for more detail. Inspect Individual Worker Logs Each worker writes its own log at runs/runX/guess.log , for example runs/run1/guess.log . These logs show which gridcells that worker processed, how long they took, and any warnings or errors encountered. When a run is unexpectedly slow, incomplete, or unusually expensive, compare several worker logs to determine how the work was divided and where time was spent. In particular, if every guess.log lists every gridcell, check for the absolute gridlist path problem . Final Output Files and append.cmd The submission script creates a second PBS job from append.cmd . PBS schedules this job to run after the main job, but only if the main job succeeds. It combines each worker's output files into the final output/ directory. For example: runs/run1/out/lai.out ┐ runs/run2/out/lai.out ├──> output/lai.out runs/run3/out/lai.out ┘ The same process is applied to every output file. If the main job fails, the append job does not run and the individual files remain under runs/runX/out/ for diagnosis or manual recovery. Common Errors Job Takes Much Longer Than Expected One possible cause is that every worker has processed the complete gridlist instead of only its assigned gridcells. The run may otherwise appear to work, so this is easy to miss without checking the job cost and worker logs. The gridlist path must be relative When using submit_to_gadi.sh , never give the gridlist an absolute path in the instruction file. Use ./<gridlist-basename> instead. This is an exception to the general recommendation to use absolute paths for input files. For example, if the gridlist is named gridlist.txt : # Wrong: every worker reads the complete, original gridlist file_gridlist "/scratch/pt17/my/input/gridlist.txt" # Correct: every worker reads its assigned part of the gridlist file_gridlist "./gridlist.txt" The parameter name depends on the input module; for example, it may be file_gridlist or file_gridlist_cf . The same rule applies in either case, and the relative filename must match the basename of the original gridlist. The submission script splits the gridlist between the runs/run1/ ... runs/runN/ directories. During a parallel run, each worker changes into its own directory and should read the split gridlist stored there. An absolute path bypasses that file, causing every worker to process the complete original gridlist. This can multiply the job's cost and cause it to exceed its requested walltime. See Path Considerations for more detail. libnetcdf.so.15: cannot open shared object file Example: /home/590/am8995/code/lpjg_aaron/build/guess: error while loading shared libraries: libnetcdf.so.15: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory This means the executable was compiled against a NetCDF library that is not available in the environment where the model is being run. The most common cause is forgetting to load the netcdf module before running. It can also happen if the model was compiled with one NetCDF module version but run with a different one. Fix: Use ./build_gadi to compile the model. It loads the required Gadi modules, including the default netcdf module. Submit runs with submit_to_gadi.sh , which generates a PBS script that loads the same kind of runtime environment before launching guess . If running manually for a quick test, load NetCDF first: bash module purge module load openmpi gcc cmake netcdf ./build/guess -input nc /path/to/simulation.ins If the error persists, check which modules are loaded in the job output: module list Then rebuild and rerun in a clean, consistent environment: module purge ./build_gadi submit_to_gadi.sh: command not found The DAVE helper scripts are probably not on your PATH . Add the shared DAVE startup file to ~/.bashrc as described in DAVE Shared Environment , then log out and back in or run: source ~/.bashrc Paths Containing ~ Do Not Work in the Configuration File The submission script reads paths from the configuration file literally. Use ${HOME} or a full path instead of ~ : BINARY=${HOME}/lpj-guess-dave/build/guess Job Starts but Cannot Read or Write Files First check that input and output paths exist and are on a filesystem available to the PBS job. Use /scratch/<project>/$USER for run outputs, not $HOME . If you wrote your own PBS script, make sure it declares the filesystems it uses, for example: #PBS -l storage=scratch/pt17 The submit_to_gadi.sh script handles this for standard runs. See Storage for more detail. Job Stops Near the Requested Walltime PBS kills jobs that exceed their walltime request. Gadi also has a maximum 48-hour walltime for a single job. Increase NPROCESS so the run finishes sooner, increase WALLTIME if it was set too low, or split the simulation into smaller jobs. See Choosing CPU Count and Walltime .

docs.text: Version Control via the Command Line This page covers the Git workflow for contributing to LPJ-GUESS DAVE using the terminal. It assumes familiarity with basic Git concepts (commits, branches, remotes). For a gentler introduction, see Version Control via SourceTree . Clone the Repository git clone git@stormbringer4.nateko.lu.se:dave/lpj-guess-dave.git lpj-guess-dave cd lpj-guess-dave The default branch after cloning is lpjguess_dave . Create a Branch Always work on a dedicated branch, not directly on lpjguess_dave : git switch -c my-feature-branch Use a short, descriptive name with hyphens (e.g. fix-canopy-conductance , add-thome-docs ). Check Status and Review Changes git status # which files have changed git diff # unstaged changes (line-by-line) git diff --staged # changes already staged for commit Stage and Commit Stage specific files you want to include in the next commit: git add path/to/changed/file.cpp path/to/file2.h git add docs/howto/my-page.md Or stage everything in the working tree (use with care): git add -A # stage all changes in the repository, including deletions git add . # stage all changes in the current directory and subdirectories git add -p # interactive patch staging — recommended over git add . Then commit with a message that describes what changed and why: git commit -m "Fix negative VPD crash when RH input is 1.0" Good commit messages use the imperative present tense and explain why the change was made, not just which files were touched. Push the Branch git push -u origin my-feature-branch The -u flag sets the upstream tracking reference so that subsequent git push and git pull calls on this branch need no arguments. Bring a Branch Up to Date Two common workflows are covered below: Bring a long-lived development branch up to date with origin/lpjguess_dave . Pull commits you made to the same branch from another machine. In both workflows, commit or stash local uncommitted changes first. Workflow A: Update from lpjguess_dave (Rebase Recommended) From your development branch: git fetch origin git rebase origin/lpjguess_dave If conflicts occur, resolve them and continue: git add <resolved-file> git rebase --continue If you already pushed the branch earlier, rebase rewrites commit hashes, so you may need: git push --force-with-lease Workflow A (Alternative): Update from lpjguess_dave with Merge If you do not want to rewrite branch history: git fetch origin git merge origin/lpjguess_dave If conflicts occur, resolve them and continue: git add <resolved-file> git merge --continue If your Git version does not support git merge --continue , complete the merge with: git commit Workflow B: Pull Your Own Branch Changes from Another Machine If you pushed commits from machine A and now want them on machine B: git switch my-feature-branch git pull This works because the branch tracks origin/my-feature-branch (set when you first used git push -u origin my-feature-branch ). Rebase vs Merge (What’s the Difference?) rebase replays your branch commits on top of the latest origin/lpjguess_dave , producing a linear history. merge creates a merge commit that ties both histories together, preserving the exact original branch timeline. Practical guidance: Prefer rebase for a clean, linear feature branch history before opening an MR. Prefer merge when you want to avoid history rewriting, especially on shared branches. Avoid rebasing commits that others have already based work on. Open a Merge Request After pushing, open the repository in your browser on GitLab. GitLab will show a banner prompting you to create a Merge Request for the branch you just pushed. Set Target branch to lpjguess_dave . Alternatively, GitLab prints a direct MR creation link in the output of git push : remote: To create a merge request for my-feature-branch, visit: remote: https://gitlab.com/.../merge_requests/new?merge_request[source_branch]=my-feature-branch The CI pipeline runs automatically. The MR can be merged once the pipeline passes and a reviewer has approved it. Note Subsequent pushes to the same branch update the open MR automatically — no need to open a new one. docs.text: Using land-cover change in DAVE This guide configures a DAVE site simulation with natural vegetation, managed forest, and optionally pasture. It assumes the usual non-crop DAVE workflow. For the model concepts, see Land cover and land-use change . Choose the mode The committed benchmarks/ozflux/settings.ins imports benchmarks/ozflux/landcover.ins , which sets run_landcover 0 . Use that setting for a site with one ordinary stand and no prescribed land-cover fractions. The file_lu parameter is ignored in this mode. For a run with prescribed fractions, add a site-specific instruction file after the shared OzFlux settings import and set run_landcover 1 . Turn on only the classes to be simulated, and define at least one included st for each active class. A class can have several stand types; the st name is used in stand-type fraction and gross-transition column headers. Keep crop disabled for a DAVE run without crops. ! In the site-specific instruction file, imported after ../settings.ins run_landcover 1 run_natural 1 run_forest 1 run_pasture 0 run_crop 0 run_urban 0 run_peatland 0 run_barren 0 st "Forest" ( common_stand stinclude 1 landcover "forest" naturalveg "all" harvest_system "continuous" ) The shared OzFlux land-cover file already defines st "Natural" . Its exact name matters for a Natural_Forest gross-transition column. If you enable pasture, also define an included pasture stand type and its appropriate PFTs and grazing settings. A managed forest stand type needs management choices suited to the experiment; the snippet is an area-configuration example. To initialise a forest stand from observed tree cohorts in a chosen year, see Prescribed tree establishment . Supply the net fractions Set file_lu to a text file of grid-cell fractions. For an annual site input, use a Lon Lat Year header followed by land-cover names in uppercase. Match the longitude and latitude to the site's file_gridlist . Values are fractions of the entire grid cell, from 0 to 1. Give one row per year and location; keep the classes summing to 1. This minimal non-crop example moves 0.10 of the grid cell from natural vegetation to forest in 1902: Lon Lat Year NATURAL FOREST 150.723611 -33.615278 1901 1.00 0.00 150.723611 -33.615278 1902 0.90 0.10 150.723611 -33.615278 1903 0.90 0.10 param "file_lu" (str "my-landcover.txt") Omitted inactive classes contribute zero. Include a column for every active class, even when its fraction is zero in some years. The reader supports other text input layouts, including year-only data shared by grid cells; the Lon Lat Year form makes a site file self-contained. File paths are resolved from the run's working directory, so run from the site directory as described in Running Serially . When run_landcover 1 has no file_lu , the model gives the active classes equal fixed fractions. That is useful for a controlled test, but is usually not useful behaviour. If only NATURAL is active, it occupies the whole grid cell. When active fractions do not sum to one, the reader may rescale them or assign unrepresented area to NATURAL ; do not rely on that correction for intended land use. Inspect log warnings and frac_sts.out . Decide whether to give gross transitions For a straightforward conversion with one donor and one receiver, file_lu alone can be sufficient. DAVE infers a transfer from the net change. For several simultaneous changes, or for turnover with unchanged net fractions, give an explicit gross-transition file. For stand-type transitions, set file_grossSTC and use columns named FromStandType_ToStandType , with the exact st names and case from the instruction file. Its Year is the year before the target net-fraction row: Lon Lat Year Natural_Forest Forest_Natural 150.723611 -33.615278 1901 0.10 0.00 150.723611 -33.615278 1902 0.00 0.00 param "file_grossSTC" (str "my-stand-transfers.txt") param "file_grossLUC" (str "") The 1901 gross row creates the 1902 net fractions in the example above. A missing transfer column is treated as zero, so check spelling carefully. Each transfer is a fraction of the entire grid cell. Before running, verify for each year and stand type that incoming minus outgoing transfers equals the change in its net fraction . For a class with several stand types, also check that their target fractions add to the class fraction. file_grossLUC is a different, LUH-style, land-cover-level transfer format with short category columns such as vp and pv ; it is not a table of Natural_Forest columns. DAVE maps these class transfers to stand types and may adjust inconsistent gross transfers to match net fractions. Use file_grossSTC when the donor and receiver stand types are known. If both gross paths are configured, file_grossLUC wins, so keep the unused path empty. If a land-cover class contains multiple stand types, the optional file_lunatural , file_luforest , or file_lupasture supplies their fractions over time. Without such a file, active stand types in that class have equal shares. A stand-type fraction file uses stand-type names as columns. The reader infers whether its values are shares within the class or absolute grid-cell fractions by checking whether the numeric columns sum to one. Use one convention consistently across cells and years, and confirm the reported stand-type areas in frac_sts.out . For a single stand type in each class, these extra files are unnecessary. Stand transfer settings The shared benchmarks/ozflux/landcover.ins defines the following settings. Override only those needed by the experiment: Setting Effect npatch_secondarystand Number of replicate patches in a newly created secondary stand. reduce_all_stands If 0 , use age and destination rules to choose donor stands; if 1 , reduce stands more evenly. age_limit_reduce Age threshold used when selecting stands to shrink. transfer_level Pool transferred state across the grid cell ( 0 ), land-cover class ( 1 ), or stand type ( 2 ). iftransfer_to_new_stand Allow eligible converted areas to become separate stands, with vegetation carried over or cleared according to the receiving stand's settings. ifslowharvestpool Include the slow harvested-product pool in land-cover harvest accounting. ifprimary_lc_transfer and ifprimary_to_secondary_transfer are for detailed primary/secondary transition data; leave them at 0 for the simple stand-type example. harvest_secondary_to_new_stand controls a wood-harvest path that can create secondary stands, even with no change in broad class area. Harvest, planting, and disturbance settings can therefore change the result of an area transition. See Disturbance when prescribed fire, wind, bark beetle, or clearcut input is also active. Run and inspect Run the site instruction file from its directory. With the standard build and NetCDF climate input, the form is: cd benchmarks/ozflux/<SiteName> ../../../build/guess -input nc <SiteName>.ins Add output settings to the site-specific instruction file. These are useful starting points: file_frac_sts "frac_sts.out" file_nstand_sts "nstand_sts.out" file_cmass_sts "cmass_sts.out" file_luc_cflux_sts "luc_cflux_sts.out" file_cflux_natural "cflux_natural.out" file_cflux_forest "cflux_forest.out" frac_sts.out reports stand-type fractions, class fractions, and a grid-cell total. nstand_sts.out reports how many runtime stands represent each type; its count can increase after a transfer even if the type's area does not. cmass_sts.out helps distinguish area changes from changes in vegetation carbon. luc_cflux_sts.out and the class carbon-flux files help check the carbon consequences of conversion. Set printstandtypes 1 for stand-type columns; printseparatestands 1 requests individual stand output where supported, but the model disables it for land-cover files covering more than 100 grid cells to avoid too many files. Output is written under the configured outputdirectory . Check the first input year, the first year in which fractions change, and the year after the last supplied row. Compare frac_sts.out with the intended fractions, and check that an explicit gross row dated \(y-1\) produces the expected transition into year \(y\) . During spin-up, land-cover changes can be held until the soil spin-up threshold; read the log for the first active year. Common input problems If the fractions, transfers, or carbon fluxes look wrong, check guess.log in the site run directory first . Search for the affected year, stand type, rescaling messages, warnings, and errors. Set verbosity 3 in the .ins file for informational land-cover messages; 4 or 5 can provide more detail. See Start with guess.log . Symptom What to check All active land covers must have at least one stand type Define an included st with the matching landcover for every run_* 1 class. Missing input or a site excluded Check file_lu path, Lon / Lat against file_gridlist , and that the file has data for the location. Fraction-sum or rescaling warning Check all active columns, their units, and that each year's fractions sum to one. No change in the expected year Check the initial row, spin-up timing, and the one-year offset of the gross file. Wrong or missing donor stand Check gross column names against st names and balance gross transfers against net stand-type fractions. Unexpected carbon flux or number of stands Inspect harvest, disturbance, transfer_level , and iftransfer_to_new_stand as well as the area files. The repository's benchmarks/ozflux/CumberlandPlain/ directory contains a larger cup.luc.txt and cup.gross_stc.txt example with both directions of natural/forest conversion. Its site instruction imports cup.luc.ins after the shared settings; use it as a worked example and adjust the years, location, management, and input paths for your own site.

docs.text: Management types for natural and forest stands A stand type describes an area of a grid cell, its land cover, and the management regimes it may use. A management type ( mt ) is a named set of rules for that stand: which plant functional types (PFTs) may be planted or establish, when and how trees are cut, and whether disturbance is suppressed. Each stand contains one or more replicate patches. Patch ages and vegetation can differ even when their stand type and management type are the same. Management rules become relevant when land-cover mode ( run_landcover 1 ) is used. Normal forest cutting is evaluated for natural and forest stands at the start of each year. Treeinit can use these same regimes to specify what happens after its one-time replacement. Harvesting and vegetation removal explains where biomass goes when a cut occurs; land-cover change explains how stand area changes. Assign a regime Define an mt block and assign it to a stand type with management1 . management2 and management3 are optional later regimes. In a treeinit stand, management2 is required: treeinit switches affected stands to it after installing the prescribed trees. The second regime can allow subsequent growth without scheduled cutting, or prescribe later thinning and cutting. Treeinit also adds the PFTs named in its input file to the second regime's selection. Set cutfirstyear 0 if the new regime should preserve the trees through its first year. mt "Before_initialisation" ( harvest_system "continuous" cutfirstyear 0 ) mt "After_initialisation" ( planting_system "selection" selection "MRS" reestab "restricted" harvest_system "continuous" cutfirstyear 0 ) st "Forest" ( common_stand stinclude 1 landcover "forest" naturalveg "all" management1 "Before_initialisation" management2 "After_initialisation" file_treeinit_st "forest-treeinit.txt" ) An alternative is to place management settings directly in st ; these apply to its first regime. Prefer named mt blocks when using several regimes, and avoid mixing inline first-regime settings with a named management1 because the named regime takes precedence. mtinclude 0 excludes a named management type from the run. Stand-type keys mt1_startyear , mt2_startyear , and mt3_startyear set calendar years for normal regime rotation; rotation_wait_for_cc 1 waits for a clearcut before switching under a clearcut system. Treeinit makes its own switch to regime 2 at the event. Core choices planting_system determines which tree PFTs are planted after cutting. An empty value leaves the stand's eligible tree PFTs available. "selection" uses the names in selection ; "monoculture" uses pft . Other supported values select broad groups such as evergreen needleleaf or deciduous broadleaf trees. reestab "all" permits eligible PFTs to establish later; "restricted" limits tree reestablishment to planted PFTs, and "none" prevents tree reestablishment. The stand type's landcover and naturalveg settings still define the outer set of eligible vegetation. See Establishment for climatic establishment limits. harvest_system "clearcut" uses rotations and optional intermediate thinnings. "continuous" schedules repeated partial cutting and may use a second cutting period. "probability_input" uses externally supplied cutting probabilities and intensities. An empty harvest system has no normal scheduled wood cutting; other events, including land-cover conversion and treeinit, may still remove vegetation. Parameters below are activated by the system or feature they describe; specifying a thinning strength alone does not schedule a cut. Management-type parameter reference Values in the same row are related but remain separate input parameters. Years described as calendar years use the model's calendar, while intervals and patch ages count elapsed years. Fractions generally range from 0 to 1. Unless stated otherwise, switches use 0 for off and 1 for on. Selection, establishment, and grazing Parameter Meaning planting_system Planting rule: empty, selection , monoculture , or a supported tree group. selection Space-separated PFT names used for selected planting and preferential cutting. pft Single PFT for monoculture planting; also used by crop regimes. plantdensity , plantdensity_pft Seedlings per hectare for selected PFTs, or the single pft , respectively. set_planting_density Use specified tree planting densities after a clearcut and bypass environmental establishment limits for that planting. reestab all , restricted , or none : controls later tree establishment after planting. relaxed_establishment Ignore climatic limits on establishment once management starts. stochmort , stochestab Enable stochastic mortality or establishment, respectively. Both default to on. grazeintens Daily grazing fraction for managed grass vegetation. For managed grassland, mowdates (day-of-year values) and mowintens (fraction removed) can also be set inline in st . They are not accepted inside a named mt block. The default is 1 ; set this explicitly for treeinit stands. cutfirstyear_unsel Also cut PFTs outside the new selection on entry or cloning. cutinterval Main rotation or cutting interval in years. delayduecutting Spread overdue density-triggered clearcuts over this many years after firstclearcutyear . distribute_patch_ages Stagger patch ages in a newly managed forest stand. distribute_cuttings_among_patches Stagger cutting events among patches. Cutting systems and thinnings Parameter Meaning harvest_system clearcut , continuous , probability_input , or empty. External probability inputs require their own forcing files. thintime One or more thinning times as fractions of the first rotation or cutting period. thinstrength , thinstrength_unsel Fractions cut at corresponding thintime entries for selected and unselected PFTs. thinselectpft PFT preference at thinning: 0 none, 1 unselected, 2 selected, 3 separate selected/unselected strengths, 4 shrubs and shade-intolerant PFTs. thinselectage Age preference: 0 none, 1 younger, 2 older trees. thinselectdiam Diameter preference: 0 none, 1 smaller, 2 larger, 3 diameter-limit cutting. secondintervalstart Years after the first period begins at which continuous cutting enters its second period. secondcutinterval Cutting interval in that second period. secondthintime , secondthinstrength , secondthinstrength_unsel Second-period counterparts of the first-period thinning times and strengths. secondthinselectpft , secondthinselectage , secondthinselectdiam Second-period counterparts of the PFT, age, and diameter preferences. diam_cut_low , diam_cut_high Diameter thresholds in centimetres for diameter-limit cutting; between them partial cutting applies and above the high limit all eligible trees are cut. adapt_diam_limit Adjust the low diameter threshold for stands with small trees. ifthin_reineke Use automatic thinning based on Reineke's stand-density rule. alpha_st , rdi_target Self-thinning coefficient and target relative density for Reineke thinning; a lower density target means stronger thinning. ifclearcut_by_density , dens_target_cc Enable clearcut when tree density falls below the specified trees-per-hectare threshold. ifclearcut_optimal_age Use the model's optimal rotation age as a clearcut trigger. killgrass_at_cc Remove grass vegetation during clearcut. A relative thinning time of 0.5 means halfway through the relevant period. Density and optimal-age triggers apply to clearcut management; if several triggers are set, the model resolves their priority internally, so avoid assuming all will cause independent cuts. Parameter Meaning targetfrac Target biomass fractions corresponding to PFTs in selection . file_targetfrac_pft_mt File supplying time-varying PFT target fractions. targetfrac_input_mode 0 use file fractions for cutting, retain instruction-file selection; 1 use file fractions and restrict selection to PFTs with nonzero fractions; 2 use file fractions only to define selection, without target cutting. firsttargetyear , lasttargetyear Calendar-year window for target cutting. targetstartage , targetcutinterval Minimum patch age and years between target cuts. targetcutmode 1 calculate deviations at patch level; 2 or 3 use stand-level deviations. targetthinselectage , targetthinselectdiam Prefer younger/older ( 0 / 1 / 2 ) or smaller/larger ( 0 / 1 / 2 ) individuals during target cutting. The six harvest and residue values default to unset . Stem efficiency and twig removal then use PFT-level settings; coarse-root removal defaults to 0.1. They affect normal management cuts, not the one-time vegetation removal performed by treeinit. See Harvesting and vegetation removal for the resulting biomass pathways. They describe crop water supply, sowing and harvest dates, nitrogen fertilisation, tillage, and fallow. They are listed here for completeness but are outside the DAVE natural/forest workflow.
docs.title: Management Types

docs.text: A stand type describes an area of a grid cell, its land cover, and the management regimes it may use. A management type ( mt ) is a named set of rules for that stand: which plant functional types (PFTs) may be planted or establish, when and how trees are cut, and whether disturbance is suppressed. Each stand contains one or more replicate patches. Patch ages and vegetation can differ even when their stand type and management type are the same. Management rules become relevant when land-cover mode ( run_landcover 1 ) is used. Normal forest cutting is evaluated for natural and forest stands at the start of each year. Treeinit can use these same regimes to specify what happens after its one-time replacement. Harvesting and vegetation removal explains where biomass goes when a cut occurs; land-cover change explains how stand area changes.
docs.title: Management types for natural and forest stands

docs.text: Define an mt block and assign it to a stand type with management1 . management2 and management3 are optional later regimes. In a treeinit stand, management2 is required: treeinit switches affected stands to it after installing the prescribed trees. The second regime can allow subsequent growth without scheduled cutting, or prescribe later thinning and cutting. Treeinit also adds the PFTs named in its input file to the second regime's selection. Set cutfirstyear 0 if the new regime should preserve the trees through its first year. mt "Before_initialisation" ( harvest_system "continuous" cutfirstyear 0 ) mt "After_initialisation" ( planting_system "selection" selection "MRS" reestab "restricted" harvest_system "continuous" cutfirstyear 0 ) st "Forest" ( common_stand stinclude 1 landcover "forest" naturalveg "all" management1 "Before_initialisation" management2 "After_initialisation" file_treeinit_st "forest-treeinit.txt" ) An alternative is to place management settings directly in st ; these apply to its first regime. Prefer named mt blocks when using several regimes, and avoid mixing inline first-regime settings with a named management1 because the named regime takes precedence. mtinclude 0 excludes a named management type from the run. Stand-type keys mt1_startyear , mt2_startyear , and mt3_startyear set calendar years for normal regime rotation; rotation_wait_for_cc 1 waits for a clearcut before switching under a clearcut system. Treeinit makes its own switch to regime 2 at the event.
docs.title: Assign a regime

docs.text: planting_system determines which tree PFTs are planted after cutting. An empty value leaves the stand's eligible tree PFTs available. "selection" uses the names in selection ; "monoculture" uses pft . Other supported values select broad groups such as evergreen needleleaf or deciduous broadleaf trees. reestab "all" permits eligible PFTs to establish later; "restricted" limits tree reestablishment to planted PFTs, and "none" prevents tree reestablishment. The stand type's landcover and naturalveg settings still define the outer set of eligible vegetation. See Establishment for climatic establishment limits. harvest_system "clearcut" uses rotations and optional intermediate thinnings. "continuous" schedules repeated partial cutting and may use a second cutting period. "probability_input" uses externally supplied cutting probabilities and intensities. An empty harvest system has no normal scheduled wood cutting; other events, including land-cover conversion and treeinit, may still remove vegetation. Parameters below are activated by the system or feature they describe; specifying a thinning strength alone does not schedule a cut.
docs.title: Core choices

docs.text: Values in the same row are related but remain separate input parameters. Years described as calendar years use the model's calendar, while intervals and patch ages count elapsed years. Fractions generally range from 0 to 1. Unless stated otherwise, switches use 0 for off and 1 for on.

Writing Equations in Markdown This page is a practical reference for writing mathematical equations on this documentation site. If you are familiar with Word's equation editor but new to LaTeX, start here. Equations are written in LaTeX syntax, which is the standard for typesetting mathematics in scientific publishing. The site renders them automatically wherever you write them. Inline vs Display Equations There are two ways to include an equation: Type Syntax When to use Inline $...$ Part of a sentence, e.g. "where \(x\) is…" Display $$...$$ Standalone, centred equation on its own line Inline example — the source: The leaf area index $L$ is the one-sided area of leaf tissue per unit ground area (m² m⁻²). renders as: The leaf area index \(L\) is the one-sided area of leaf tissue per unit ground area (m² m⁻²). Display example — the source: $$ E = mc^2 $$ renders as: \[ E = mc^2 \] Tip Use display equations for anything that has multiple terms, fractions, or needs to be easy to refer to. Use inline for short symbols and simple expressions that flow naturally in a sentence. docs.text: Migrating from the Old Upstream LPJ-GUESS Repository This is for people who previously worked on the original/core LPJ-GUESS repo and want to repoint their existing local clone to this new Australian team fork. If you’re cloning fresh, skip this section. 1. Check current remote git remote -v You’ll likely see something like: origin git@stormbringer4.nateko.lu.se:lpj-guess-developers/LPJ-GUESS.git (fetch) origin git@stormbringer4.nateko.lu.se:lpj-guess-developers/LPJ-GUESS.git (push) 2. Commit any local work Make sure no work is lost: git status If you see uncommitted changes: git add <files> git commit -m "Save work before migration" 3. Point origin to the new team fork Replace the URL below with the actual team fork URL: git remote set-url origin git@stormbringer4.nateko.lu.se:dave/lpj-guess-dave.git Verify: git remote -v We intentionally do not keep a remote pointing to the old upstream, to avoid accidental pushes. 4. Push your branches to the new fork List local branches: git branch Push each branch you care about: git checkout <branch-name> git push -u origin <branch-name> 5. Rename your long-lived branch (optional but recommended) If your main working branch was not named lpjguess_dave_<your_name> : git checkout <old-branch> git branch -m lpjguess_dave_<your_name> git push -u origin lpjguess_dave_<your_name> git push origin --delete <old-branch> # optional Ask a maintainer before deleting branches on the remote. 6. Final checks git fetch , git pull , and git push should work normally. git branch -a should show: lpjguess_dave trunk your lpjguess_dave_<name> branch At this point, you’re fully migrated and can follow the primary workflow in Contributing Code (Workflow) . If you have improvements to suggest, please open an Issue titled: “Update CONTRIBUTING / migration docs”

docs.text: OzFlux Site Simulations This page describes the input file structure for the OzFlux site-level simulations included in the repository under benchmarks/ozflux/ . Directory Structure benchmarks/ozflux/ ├── settings.ins # Top-level simulation switches ├── outputs.ins # Output file declarations ├── pft_dave.ins # PFT parameters (trees, grasses) ├── soiln.ins # Soil nitrogen parameters ├── forcing/ # Forcing data (climate, soil, fire, etc) ├── <SiteName>/ │ ├── <SiteName>.ins # Site-level instruction file (entry point) │ └── gridlist.txt # Lon/lat for this site └── ... Each site has its own subdirectory containing a site-level .ins file and a gridlist.txt . The site-level .ins file is short: it sets the site-specific paths and imports the shared configuration files. Shared Configuration Files All sites import the same set of common .ins files from the benchmarks/ozflux/ directory. These control parameters shared across all sites: File Contents settings.ins Top-level switches: timestep, enabled modules, scenario outputs.ins Available output variables; most are disabled by default pft_dave.ins PFT parameters for trees and grasses soiln.ins Soil nitrogen parameters To enable an output variable, open outputs.ins and uncomment the relevant line. The comment character is ! . Obtaining Climate Data The forcing data is stored on HIE-Storage and must be downloaded separately. See HIE-Storage for access details. The data should be placed at benchmarks/ozflux/forcing/ . Running a Site For a complete worked example, start with Running and Debugging via VSCode . That page shows how to run CumberlandPlain , where outputs are written, and what to check after the run. To run from the command line, see Running Serially . Outputs are written to benchmarks/ozflux/<SiteName>/out/ by default. The model log is benchmarks/ozflux/<SiteName>/guess.log . Check it first if the run fails or an output looks wrong. verbosity in the site .ins file controls its detail; the shared settings.ins sets it to 3 . See Start with guess.log for the recommended diagnostic steps.

docs.text: Prescribed tree establishment (treeinit) Treeinit places specified tree cohorts into a stand type in a chosen calendar year. Use it to initialise a stand from an observed tree size and density structure. It does not prescribe land-cover area or replace ordinary recruitment in later years. See Establishment for annual recruitment and Land cover and land-use change for stand areas. What happens At the end of init_year , after annual vegetation dynamics and prescribed disturbance, LPJ-GUESS removes the existing vegetation in each affected patch and creates the trees described by the input rows. Existing trees are cut and their biomass is divided among exported material and litter; existing grasses become litter. Harvesting and vegetation removal explains this accounting. The new trees receive size, density, age, carbon, and nitrogen state. Their added carbon and nitrogen are recorded as prescribed inputs through seed flux accounting, rather than as growth during that year. Ordinary annual establishment is skipped for this stand type in the initialisation year. The affected stands then move to management2 , the regime governing later cutting, planting, and establishment. See Management types for the concepts and parameter reference. With the default forest_init_poolsoil 0 , existing stands keep their area, patches, and soil state while their vegetation is replaced. With forest_init_poolsoil 1 , LPJ-GUESS pools the soil and other non-living state across the stands being initialised, removes those stands, and creates one new stand per affected stand type. The new stands have npatch_treeinit replicate patches. Their area can be redistributed among affected stand types using next-year fractions while their combined area is preserved. All affected stand types must have the same initialisation year when pooling is enabled. Configure the stand type Set file_treeinit_st inside the stand type to be initialised. In the land-cover workflow, use run_landcover 1 , ensure the type has positive area in init_year , and provide valid management1 and management2 regimes. Treeinit updates the second regime's PFT selection to include the PFTs in the input file. For example, in a site-specific instruction file imported after the shared OzFlux settings: run_landcover 1 run_natural 1 run_forest 1 run_crop 0 mt "Forest_before_init" ( harvest_system "continuous" cutfirstyear 0 ) mt "Forest_after_init" ( harvest_system "continuous" cutfirstyear 0 ) st "Forest" ( common_stand stinclude 1 landcover "forest" naturalveg "all" management1 "Forest_before_init" management2 "Forest_after_init" file_treeinit_st "forest-treeinit.txt" ) forest_init_from_biomass 1 forest_init_poolsoil 0 The shared OzFlux file already defines st "Natural" . Set forest area with file_lu as described in Using land-cover change . Ensure the stand permits each tree PFT named in the treeinit file. Choose the two management regimes for the experiment; treeinit does not prescribe future cutting or recruitment. Prepare the input file Use a whitespace-delimited file with one row per prescribed tree cohort . The same cohort description is applied to every affected patch of the stand type. Tree_no is a record index, starting at 0 and increasing by one; it need not identify an observed individual tree. Match Lon and Lat to the site grid list and str_pft to an included tree PFT exactly, including case. Lon Lat Tree_no init_year str_pft biomass dbh dens tree_age 150.723611 -33.615278 0 2015 MRS 0.180 18.0 450 20 150.723611 -33.615278 1 2015 MRS 0.025 8.0 900 8 Column Meaning Lon , Lat Grid-cell location. Each grid cell using this stand type needs a matching block of rows. Tree_no Consecutive cohort record index, starting at 0 ; the limit is 100 rows per location and stand type. init_year Calendar year of the one-time event. Use the same year in all rows; the first row sets it. str_pft Exact name of a tree PFT included in the run. biomass Aboveground dry biomass per representative tree, in tonnes. Required with forest_init_from_biomass 1 . dbh Diameter at breast height, in centimetres. Used as the size input with forest_init_from_biomass 0 . dens Number of trees per hectare represented by the cohort. tree_age Age in years. If absent or nonpositive, DAVE estimates it from diameter. Rows after the first describe additional cohorts for the same event , not later initialisation years. Use a separate stand type for areas that require different event years or management histories. Give every cohort a positive size and density. The file must cover every simulated grid cell for which this stand type has file_treeinit_st . forest_init_from_biomass defaults to 1 . In that mode, DAVE derives wood carbon and diameter from biomass ; the supplied dbh is not the controlling size value. With forest_init_from_biomass 0 , DAVE uses dbh and PFT allometry to calculate size and wood carbon. Supplying both columns makes the file easier to inspect and use with either setting. Supply dens explicitly: its units are converted internally from trees per hectare to trees per square metre, and the fallback for a missing value is not a site observation. Run and verify Run the model with the stand type and input file. The log reports the initialisation year and each prescribed cohort created. Enable stand-type outputs to check the area, structure, and carbon around the event: printstandtypes 1 file_frac_sts "frac_sts.out" file_nstand_sts "nstand_sts.out" file_dens_sts "dens_sts.out" file_diam_sts "diam_sts.out" file_cmass_sts "cmass_sts.out" file_dave_stand_frac "dave_stand_frac.out" file_dave_stand_type "dave_stand_type.out" Check that the stand has positive area in init_year , every intended cohort appears in the log, and density, diameter, and carbon reflect the input. Inspect the following year too, when management2 is active. If soil pooling is enabled, also inspect stand count and soil pools. The repository's benchmarks/ozflux/CumberlandPlain/cup.treeinit.txt and cup.luc.ins provide a worked example. Common problems Start with guess.log in the directory from which you ran the site (for example, benchmarks/ozflux/CumberlandPlain/guess.log ). Search for the stand type, PFT, init_year , warnings, and errors. If the reason is still unclear, set verbosity 3 or higher in the .ins file and rerun; levels 4 and 5 give progressively more detail. The shared OzFlux settings already use 3 . See Start with guess.log for a general log-reading workflow. Check the log before using the symptom-specific checks below. Symptom Check No prescribed trees appear Positive stand area in init_year , simulation reaches that year, and str_pft matches an included tree PFT. Input file fails to load File path relative to the run directory, site coordinates, and row block for every simulated grid cell. Missing biomass error Supply biomass , or set forest_init_from_biomass 0 and supply dbh . Missing management2 error Define and assign a valid second management regime. Cohorts appear wrong Use consecutive Tree_no indices from 0 , one row per cohort, and no more than 100 rows. Unexpected stand count or soil change Check forest_init_poolsoil and npatch_treeinit .

docs.text: Repository Map This page gives a practical tour of the LPJ-GUESS DAVE repository. It is written for people who need to run simulations, inspect inputs, or make small configuration changes without first learning the whole codebase. Top-Level Files Path Purpose README.md Short project description and link to this documentation site. mkdocs.yml Configuration for the documentation website. .gitlab-ci.yml GitLab pipeline: compile checks and documentation deployment. CMakeLists.txt Main build configuration for compiling the model. runozflux Convenience script for building and running many OzFlux site simulations locally. build_gadi Convenience script for compiling on Gadi with the expected module environment. Documentation Path Purpose docs/ Source files for the documentation website. docs/howto/ Practical setup, data access, running, and workflow guides. docs/science/ Science and model-process notes. docs/development/ Developer and project-organisation notes. docs/img/ Images used by the documentation site. Documentation pages are Markdown files ( .md ). After a documentation change is merged into lpjguess_dave , GitLab Pages rebuilds the published site automatically. See Contributing to the Documentation for the documentation workflow. OzFlux Simulations Most DAVE site-level work starts in: benchmarks/ozflux/ Important files and directories: Path Purpose benchmarks/ozflux/<SiteName>/<SiteName>.ins Entry point for one site simulation. benchmarks/ozflux/<SiteName>/gridlist.txt Longitude and latitude for that site. benchmarks/ozflux/settings.ins Shared model switches and run settings for OzFlux simulations. benchmarks/ozflux/outputs.ins Output file declarations. Comment or uncomment lines here to control outputs. benchmarks/ozflux/pft_dave.ins DAVE PFT parameter definitions. benchmarks/ozflux/soiln.ins Soil nitrogen settings. benchmarks/ozflux/forcing/ Large forcing data downloaded separately from HIE-Storage. benchmarks/ozflux/<SiteName>/out/ Default output directory created when a site is run. For example, the Cumberland Plain run starts from: benchmarks/ozflux/CumberlandPlain/CumberlandPlain.ins That file sets the site-specific climate file and gridlist, then imports the shared OzFlux configuration files. OzFlux Site Simulations describes this input structure in more detail, while Running and Debugging via VSCode is the practical guide to running one site. Source Code Most model source code is C++. Path Purpose framework/ Core LPJ-GUESS framework: driver, data structures, parameters, output infrastructure, and utilities. modules/ Process modules and DAVE-specific model code. This is where most scientific model changes happen. modules/daveinput.cpp DAVE NetCDF input module, selected with -input nc . modules/daveoutput.cpp DAVE output module and file_dave_* output definitions. modules/davephotosynthesis.cpp DAVE photosynthesis calculations. modules/growth.cpp Growth and allocation logic. modules/soilwater.cpp , modules/hydraulics.cpp , modules/soil.cpp Water, hydraulics, and soil-related calculations. libraries/ Small bundled support libraries used by the model. command_line_version/ Command-line executable entry point. For an overview of the DAVE NetCDF input settings, see Climate Input . The source code is not normally needed to run a site simulation, but this table can help locate the relevant area when discussing a model behaviour with a developer. Build and Test Outputs These are generated locally and normally should not be committed: Path Purpose build/ Local CMake build directory. benchmarks/ozflux/<SiteName>/out/ Simulation outputs for a site. benchmarks/ozflux/<SiteName>/state/ State files, if state saving is enabled. tests/test_outputs/ Test output files generated by some test workflows. If SourceTree or Git shows many files under build/ , out/ , or state/ , do not commit them unless a maintainer has specifically asked for those files. See Common Failures for a short explanation of this common SourceTree situation. Inputs and Outputs at a Glance A typical local OzFlux run uses this chain: benchmarks/ozflux/<SiteName>/<SiteName>.ins imports ../outputs.ins imports ../settings.ins imports ../soiln.ins reads ../forcing/met/<SiteName>.nc reads gridlist.txt writes out/*.out The model must usually be run from the site directory, for example: cd benchmarks/ozflux/CumberlandPlain ../../../build/guess -input nc CumberlandPlain.ins Running from the site directory matters because many paths in the instruction files are relative paths. Running Serially explains this convention and other command-line options; Debugging via VSCode covers the supplied graphical run configurations.

Path Purpose framework/ Core LPJ-GUESS framework: driver, data structures, parameters, output infrastructure, and utilities. modules/ Process modules and DAVE-specific model code. This is where most scientific model changes happen. modules/daveinput.cpp DAVE NetCDF input module, selected with -input nc . modules/daveoutput.cpp DAVE output module and file_dave_* output definitions. modules/davephotosynthesis.cpp DAVE photosynthesis calculations. modules/growth.cpp Growth and allocation logic. modules/soilwater.cpp , modules/hydraulics.cpp , modules/soil.cpp Water, hydraulics, and soil-related calculations. libraries/ Small bundled support libraries used by the model. command_line_version/ Command-line executable entry point. For an overview of the DAVE NetCDF input settings, see Climate Input . The source code is not normally needed to run a site simulation, but this table can help locate the relevant area when discussing a model behaviour with a developer.

docs.text: These are generated locally and normally should not be committed: Path Purpose build/ Local CMake build directory. benchmarks/ozflux/<SiteName>/out/ Simulation outputs for a site. benchmarks/ozflux/<SiteName>/state/ State files, if state saving is enabled. tests/test_outputs/ Test output files generated by some test workflows. If SourceTree or Git shows many files under build/ , out/ , or state/ , do not commit them unless a maintainer has specifically asked for those files. See Common Failures for a short explanation of this common SourceTree situation.

docs.text: A typical local OzFlux run uses this chain: benchmarks/ozflux/<SiteName>/<SiteName>.ins imports ../outputs.ins imports ../settings.ins imports ../soiln.ins reads ../forcing/met/<SiteName>.nc reads gridlist.txt writes out/*.out The model must usually be run from the site directory, for example: cd benchmarks/ozflux/CumberlandPlain ../../../build/guess -input nc CumberlandPlain.ins Running from the site directory matters because many paths in the instruction files are relative paths. Running Serially explains this convention and other command-line options; Debugging via VSCode covers the supplied graphical run configurations.

docs.text: Running on Gadi This page is the practical workflow for building and submitting an LPJ-GUESS DAVE job on the Gadi HPC system . If this is your first time using Gadi, complete Setting Up Gadi before continuing. Related guides provide more detail when you need it: Setting Up Gadi —accounts, SSH, PBS, modules, and storage Checking and Troubleshooting Gadi Runs —logs, output collation, and common errors Choosing Gadi Resources and Estimating Costs —CPU, memory, walltime, and SU estimates Before You Start You should have: access to Gadi and an NCI project such as pt17 the LPJ-GUESS-DAVE repository and your input files on Gadi the DAVE shared environment enabled a run output location under /scratch , not $HOME Connect to Gadi: ssh <nci_username>@gadi.nci.org.au Build LPJ-GUESS The repository includes a build_gadi script that loads the correct modules and compiles the model. From the repository root: ./build_gadi The script clears previously loaded modules, loads OpenMPI, GCC, CMake, and NetCDF, and creates a Release build in build/ . Use this script to avoid mismatches between the modules used to build and run LPJ-GUESS. Create a Submission Configuration Copy example.conf from the hie-dave/lpj-scripts repository as a starting point. Parameter Description Example OUT_DIR Root output directory. Use /scratch , not $HOME /scratch/pt17/some/directory BINARY Path to the compiled guess binary ${HOME}/lpj-guess-dave/build/guess EXPERIMENT Subdirectory name within OUT_DIR for this run barra2-dave NPROCESS Number of parallel workers (CPUs) 48 WALLTIME Maximum job duration ( hh:mm:ss ); no more than 48 hours 02:00:00 MEMORY Total memory allocation; use 4 GiB per CPU on normal 192GB QUEUE PBS queue normal PROJECT NCI project to charge SUs to pt17 EMAIL Address for PBS job-status notifications you@uni.edu.au EMAIL_NOTIFICATIONS 1 to receive email, 0 to suppress 1 INSFILE Path to the instruction file /scratch/pt17/my/simulation.ins INPUT_MODULE LPJ-GUESS input module; use nc for DAVE nc Do not use ~ for home-directory expansion in this file. Use ${HOME} or an absolute path instead. See Choosing Gadi Resources and Estimating Costs before selecting NPROCESS , MEMORY , and WALLTIME for a large run. Use a Relative Gridlist Path The gridlist is the exception to the absolute-path rule In the instruction file, the gridlist must use a relative path such as ./gridlist.txt . An absolute gridlist path can cause every worker to run every gridcell, making the job take much longer and cost far more than expected. The parameter may be named file_gridlist , file_gridlist_cf , or something else depending on the input module. Its value must be ./<gridlist-basename> —for example: file_gridlist "./gridlist.txt" All other input files should generally use absolute paths. See Job Takes Much Longer Than Expected for an explanation of this special case. Prepare a Dry Run For parallel production runs, use submit_to_gadi.sh from the hie-dave/lpj-scripts repository. Start with the -d option: submit_to_gadi.sh -d -s my_run.conf The required -s option identifies the configuration file. The -d option performs all preparation but does not submit jobs to PBS. The script: Creates the runs/run1/ … runs/runN/ working directories required by the parallel launcher (see Running in Parallel ). Splits the gridlist into approximately equal chunks, one per worker. Generates the MPI execution command file, which loads the build-time modules and launches LPJ-GUESS with mpirun . Generates append.cmd , which will combine the workers' output files. Inspect the generated files and, if needed, manually test a single gridcell on the login node. Keep login-node tests short and limited to one gridcell; production runs must use PBS. A brief test will usually expose invalid paths, missing instruction-file parameters, and similar startup errors immediately. Submit the Jobs Once the dry run and any single-gridcell checks succeed, submit normally: submit_to_gadi.sh -s my_run.conf The script submits two PBS jobs: The main job runs LPJ-GUESS in parallel. The append job is scheduled to run only if the main job succeeds. It combines the workers' individual output files into output/ . You can monitor or cancel the main job with standard PBS commands: qstat -u $USER qstat -f <jobid> qdel <jobid> Check the Result After the jobs finish, check these files: Path Purpose <job name>.log Top-level job log; its final lines report requested and used PBS resources and total SU cost runs/runX/guess.log Per-worker logs showing which gridcells ran, their timing, warnings, and errors runs/runX/out/ Individual worker outputs output/ Combined outputs created by append.cmd after a successful main job For example, the append job combines: runs/run1/out/lai.out ┐ runs/run2/out/lai.out ├──> output/lai.out runs/run3/out/lai.out ┘ Check the worker guess.log files first when the model fails or produces unexpected results. verbosity in the .ins file controls their detail; use at least 3 for investigation, or 4 / 5 for more detail. Check the top-level job log for PBS errors and resource usage after every run. LPJ-GUESS jobs typically cost around 0.005–0.01 SU per patch , where the total number of patches is npatch × number of gridcells . A substantially higher or lower cost should be investigated. See Checking and Troubleshooting Gadi Runs for a diagnostic workflow and Estimating LPJ-GUESS Run Cost for the full cost calculation.

docs.text: Running in Parallel (MPI) LPJ-GUESS can distribute a simulation across multiple CPU cores using MPI. This page covers general parallel execution. For running on the Gadi HPC system specifically, see Running on Gadi . Prerequisites The binary must have been compiled with MPI support. CMake detects MPI automatically if an MPI implementation (e.g. OpenMPI, MPICH) is installed. See Dependencies and Toolchains for details. Parallelisation Strategy Parallelism operates at the gridcell level . Each MPI rank is assigned a disjoint subset of gridcells from a separate gridlist file and processes them independently. There is no communication between ranks during the simulation. Consequences: Performance scales linearly with the number of processes (tested to tens of thousands of CPUs on NCI Gadi). The number of processes must not exceed the number of gridcells. Each rank writes its own output files, which must be merged after the run (see Collating Outputs below). Before Running: Directory Setup Each rank expects a subdirectory named run<N> (1-indexed) relative to the working directory where mpirun is invoked: Rank 0 → ./run1/ Rank 1 → ./run2/ ... Rank N−1 → ./runN/ Each runN/ directory must contain a gridlist file with the subset of gridcells assigned to that rank. A typical layout for 3 ranks: run_dir/ ├── run1/ │ └── gridlist.txt ├── run2/ │ └── gridlist.txt └── run3/ └── gridlist.txt Split the master gridlist into N roughly equal parts — one per directory. On Gadi, the submit_to_gadi.sh script handles this automatically (see Running on Gadi ). Path Considerations When -parallel is specified, each rank changes its working directory to its runN/ directory before the model starts. Paths in the instruction file are then resolved relative to that directory. Use absolute paths for all parameters except the gridlist. The gridlist parameter must be relative (e.g. ./gridlist.txt ) because each rank resolves it inside its own runN/ directory. Additionally, the output directory parameter must also be relative, so that each worker writes to its own output directory. All other paths (forcing files, soil data, etc.) should be absolute to avoid hard-to-diagnose path resolution failures. Running From the prepared working directory: mpirun -np <N> /absolute/path/to/build/guess -parallel -input nc /absolute/path/to/simulation.ins The -parallel flag is required to activate the MPI code paths. Omitting it while using mpirun will cause each rank to run the full simulation independently rather than cooperating. When checking a run, start with each worker's runN/guess.log (for example, run1/guess.log ) under the directory where mpirun was started. Look for warnings, errors, missing grid cells, or a worker doing unexpected work. Set verbosity 3 in the .ins file for informational messages, or 4 / 5 for more detail, then rerun if needed. See Start with guess.log . Collating Outputs Each rank writes output files (tab-separated values, .out ) into its runN/ directory. After the run, these must be merged. Since all files share the same header row, keep the header from the first rank and concatenate data rows from all others: # Example: merge aaet.out from all ranks into a single file head -1 run1/aaet.out > aaet_merged.out for dir in run*/; do tail -n +2 "${dir}aaet.out" done >> aaet_merged.out Repeat for each output variable. On Gadi, the submit_to_gadi.sh script generates and submits a merge job automatically. Output During Parallel Runs By default, progress messages from all ranks are interleaved on stdout. To force each progress line onto its own line, add to the instruction file: progress_newline 1

docs.text: Running Serially (CLI) This page explains how to run a simulation from the command line without an IDE or a debugger. Basic Syntax /path/to/build/guess -input <module> <instruction-file> For DAVE simulations, the input module is always nc (see Climate Input ): cd /path/to/repository cd benchmarks/ozflux/CumberlandPlain ../../../build/guess -input nc CumberlandPlain.ins In general, the working directory is recommended to be the same as the instruction file. This is because instruction files can contain relative paths, which are resolved relative to the working directory, but when writing instruction files, one tends to think in terms of the instruction file itself. Therefore, it's easiest to just run from the same directory as the instruction file. After every run, especially if it fails or produces unexpected output, check guess.log in the directory where you started the model (for the example, benchmarks/ozflux/CumberlandPlain/guess.log ). The .ins parameter verbosity controls its detail: use at least verbosity 3 for investigation, or 4 / 5 for more detail. See Start with guess.log for what to look for. OzFlux Sites Each OzFlux site has its own instruction file at benchmarks/ozflux/<SiteName>/<SiteName>.ins . See OzFlux Site Simulations for details of the input file structure. Useful Options Flag Description -input <module> Input module to use (typically nc when running DAVE, often cf when running upstream LPJ-GUESS with daily input) -parallel Enable MPI parallelism (requires MPI build; see parallel runs ) Compiled Binary Location After a standard CMake build the binary is at build/guess (Unix) or build\guesscmd.exe (Windows).

docs.text: SFTP via FileZilla FileZilla is a graphical SFTP client available on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Prerequisites FileZilla installed (download from filezilla-project.org ) An SSH key registered with HIE-Storage. See SSH Key Management and HIE-Storage for details. Connecting to HIE-Storage Open the Site Manager (top-left button, or File → Site Manager ). Click New site and enter the following: Field Value Protocol SFTP – SSH File Transfer Protocol Host hie-storage.sstars.ws Port (leave empty) Logon Type Key file User Your HIE-Storage username (e.g. u123456 ) Key file Path to your private key (e.g. ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 ) Click OK to save. To connect, select the site from the dropdown to the right of the Site Manager button and click Connect . Note Always select the private key file (no .pub extension), not the public key. The public key ( .pub file) is what you register with servers; the private key is what you use to authenticate. Downloading Files Navigate to the remote directory on the right-hand panel and the local destination on the left-hand panel. To download: Single file or folder : right-click → Download Multiple items : select them (Shift+click or Ctrl+click), then right-click → Download Large recursive downloads can be queued and will transfer in the background.

docs.text: SFTP via Terminal The sftp command-line client is available on Linux, macOS, and Windows (via PowerShell or MSYS2). Prerequisites An SSH key registered with HIE-Storage. See SSH Key Management and HIE-Storage for details. Connecting sftp u123456@hie-storage.sstars.ws Replace u123456 with your actual username. If your private key is not at the default location ( ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 ), specify it explicitly: sftp -i /path/to/private_key u123456@hie-storage.sstars.ws Common Commands Once connected, you are in an interactive session with two working directories: the remote (on HIE-Storage) and the local (on your machine). Command Description ls List remote directory contents lls List local directory contents cd <path> Change remote directory lcd <path> Change local directory pwd Print remote working directory lpwd Print local working directory get <file> Download a single file get -r <dir> Download a directory recursively mget <pattern> Download files matching a glob pattern put <file> Upload a single file exit Close the connection Example: Downloading OzFlux Forcing Data sftp u123456@hie-storage.sstars.ws sftp> cd /data/hiestorage/WorkingData/MEDLYN_GROUP/PROJECTS/dynamics_simulations/lpj-guess/forcing/ozflux sftp> lcd /path/to/lpj-guess-dave/benchmarks/ozflux sftp> get -r processed forcing sftp> exit This downloads the processed directory and saves it locally as forcing . Non-Interactive Download with scp For scripted or single-command transfers, scp -r is often more convenient than sftp : scp -r u123456@hie-storage.sstars.ws:/path/to/remote/dir /local/destination/
